scams.name: The Kabukicho Bottakuri Bar Overcharge
scams.description: A street tout offers 'first drink free' or 'cheap beer' and leads you into a basement or upper-floor bar. After two or three drinks, the bill reaches ¥130,000 to ¥510,000 with staff blocking the door. Shinjuku Police logged approximately 190 complaints totaling roughly ¥140 million in the first ten months of 2024 alone.
scams.avoidance: Never follow a street tout in Kabukicho, Roppongi, Shibuya, or Ikebukuro. Pick bars yourself from Google Maps with 4.5+ stars and 100+ English reviews. Demand a printed menu with yen prices before ordering. Carry only cash you plan to spend. If overcharged, call 110 and say 'bottakuri' or dispute via credit card the same day. Do not sign any slip or receipt.

scams.name: The Kabukicho Drink-Spike + Face ID Crypto Drain
scams.description: A friendly tout named 'Ron' or 'Ken' invites you to a bar where your second drink is stronger than expected. You wake at 6 a.m. with an empty wallet—and if crypto was on your phone, your Coinbase or MetaMask wallet has been drained via Face ID. One documented case involved a $20,000 cryptocurrency loss.
scams.avoidance: Turn off Face ID and Touch ID on your phone before going out at night; require a 6+ digit PIN instead. Never leave your drink unattended. Keep crypto on a hardware wallet in your hotel safe. If suddenly intoxicated, walk to the Kabukicho koban or flag a police officer. Do not settle the bill—leave immediately. If drugged, go to a hospital for a medical record before contacting police.
scams.location: Kabukicho bars, Shinjuku Kuyakusho-mae alleys, Golden Gai perimeter

scams.name: The Violent Shinjuku Tout Ambush
scams.description: A man in a puffer jacket blocks your path with photos of girls on a smartphone. When you try to walk around, he sidesteps to stay in front of you. This has escalated to physical attacks, with touts locking exits and robbing customers. Tokyo Metropolitan Police made 390+ kyakuhiki arrests in 2024.
scams.avoidance: Do not stop walking or make eye contact with touts. Walk on well-lit main drags rather than side streets after midnight. If blocked, loudly say '警察を呼ぶ' (keisatsu o yobu—I'll call the police) and walk past. If physically grabbed, shout to draw attention. Travel in groups of two or more after dark. Use Shinjuku City's anti-kyakuhiki reporting line.
scams.location: Kabukicho Central Road, Shokuan-dori, Okubo Park perimeter, Golden Gai alleys

scams.name: The Matching-App Bar Lure
scams.description: You match on Tinder, Bumble, Pairs, or Tapple with someone who suggests 'a nice bar I know' in Kabukicho or Nishi-Azabu. After one or two drinks, the bill is ¥70,000 to ¥1,100,000. The person was paid per delivered customer. In May 2025, police reported a ring that netted ¥80 million from 50+ male victims.
scams.avoidance: Insist on a venue YOU pick from Google Maps with 4.5+ stars and 100+ English reviews. If the match refuses your suggestion more than once, unmatch immediately. Meet for coffee or a walk in daylight first. Never let a matching-app meetup lead to an unvetted bar. If inside and the menu has no prices, stand up and leave before ordering. Call Tokyo Metropolitan Police Shinjuku Division and say 'マッチングアプリ ぼったくり'.

scams.name: The Yurakucho / Ginza 'HAMANOKA'-style Yakitori Overcharge
scams.description: A staff member waves you into a yakitori spot under the JR tracks. No English menu appears until after you're seated. What seemed reasonable becomes a bill 2–3x higher with otoshi charges, seat charges, and drinks you don't remember ordering. Victims report paying over ¥10,000 for two people for three non-alcoholic drinks and small plates.
scams.avoidance: Pick your yakitori from Google Maps or Tabelog with 4.0+ stars and recent Japanese reviews before leaving your hotel. Ask 'Seat料はいくらですか?' before ordering. Demand an itemized receipt—this is your legal right. Avoid places claiming Torikizoku affiliation; 15 people were arrested in January 2024 for this impersonation. Dispute with your credit card company the same day if overcharged.
scams.location: Yurakucho, Ginza back streets, Shinbashi under-the-tracks yakitori

scams.name: The Narita / Haneda Unlicensed 'Shirotaku' Taxi
scams.description: Before reaching the official taxi queue at Haneda or Narita, a man in a suit offers a 'fixed price' ride to Shinjuku in a white-plated car. There is no commercial insurance, no meter, and the quoted price often increases on arrival. A legitimate flat-rate taxi from Haneda to Shinjuku is ¥8,300; unlicensed taxis charge significantly more. Police reported 113 shirotaku arrests in Jan–Oct 2025—a 10x increase over 2021.
scams.avoidance: Use only the official airport taxi queue. Green license plates indicate legal taxis; white plates indicate illegal shirotaku. Official Haneda to Shinjuku flat rate is ¥8,300 (zone A) as of 2025; Narita to Shinjuku is approximately ¥22,500. Use Uber Japan or the Go app for transparent pricing. Better yet, take the Keikyu or Tokyo Monorail from Haneda (¥600) or Narita Express (¥3,270). Never share your hotel address with someone who approached you first.
scams.location: Narita Airport (Terminals 2 and 3), Haneda Airport (Terminal 3 arrivals), Ginza and Shibuya hotel pickups

scams.name: The Fake Monk / Bracelet Donation Scam
scams.description: A person in saffron robes (sometimes grey) presses a small gold plastic bracelet or prayer card into your hand near Sensoji's Thunder Gate or other major temples. A donation book then appears—the 'gift' suddenly costs ¥3,000 to ¥10,000. Ueno Toshogu Shrine issued a July 2023 public warning specifically calling this out, noting the scammer has no shrine affiliation.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands firmly in your pockets or holding your bag strap when passing someone in religious robes near tourist sites. Do NOT accept anything placed in your hand—drop it back immediately. Walk briskly away if they insist; they will not follow more than 20 meters. Real donations are made INSIDE temples at saisen-bako (offering boxes), never on the street. Use the official merchandise counter (授与所) inside temples if you wish to genuinely support them.
scams.location: Asakusa (Sensoji/Nakamise approach), Ueno Toshogu Shrine grounds, Shibuya Scramble Crossing, Meiji Jingu perimeter

scams.name: The Tokyo Taxi Nighttime Detour
scams.description: You hail a taxi at 2 a.m. outside a Roppongi club for a ¥1,200 ride to your hotel, but it becomes ¥4,500 with an unexplained detour. The driver gestures 'construction' or 'one way' when questioned. While Tokyo taxis are generally honest, detours concentrate between 22:00 and 05:00 when the legal 20% late-night surcharge applies and scrutiny is reduced.
scams.avoidance: Use the Go or S.RIDE app for pre-set fares and tracked drivers. Show your destination to the driver in Japanese address format via Google Maps BEFORE entering. Follow the route on your phone in real time and speak up if it diverges. Ask for the ryoshusho (receipt)—they must provide one with the company's dispute line. Plan to be home before the last train (around 00:30) or stay out until the first train (around 05:00).
scams.location: Roppongi, Ginza, Kabukicho pickups 22:00–05:00; Shibuya nighttime

scams.name: The Tourist-Area Photographer / Guide Deposit Ghost
scams.description: You book a 'freelance Tokyo photographer' on Instagram for a kimono shoot at Sensoji. You pay a ¥15,000–¥40,000 deposit. They show up, take photos, and then ghost—no edited images, no replies, and the Instagram account disappears within a week. Photography services are not covered by standard travel platform refund policies.
scams.avoidance: Book only through platforms with built-in refund protection: Airbnb Experiences, Klook, Viator, or GetYourGuide—avoid direct Instagram DMs. Pay by credit card (not debit, cash, or transfer) for chargeback protection. Verify the photographer's Instagram is at least one year old with consistent posting. Reverse-image-search portfolio shots to check for stolen images. Video-call the photographer before paying. Keep deposits small (¥5,000 or less) with balance due on delivery of edited files.
scams.location: Shibuya Scramble, Asakusa, Shinjuku Gyoen, Instagram-spot lists for 'Tokyo photographer'
